## Solution

**Claim.** A power series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k(x-c)^k$ converges uniformly on $(-\infty,\infty)$ if and only if it is a polynomial, i.e., only finitely many of the $a_k$ are nonzero.

---

### Proof of Necessity

Suppose $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k(x-c)^k$ converges uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$. Let

$$f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k(x-c)^k, \qquad S_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k(x-c)^k.$$

By the definition of uniform convergence, for any $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n \geq N$ and all $x \in \mathbb{R}$,

$$|f(x) - S_n(x)| < \varepsilon. \tag{$\ast$}$$

Fix such an $N$. For any integer $m > N$ and any $x \in \mathbb{R}$, apply $(\ast)$ with $n = N$ and $n = m$, then use the triangle inequality:

$$|S_m(x) - S_N(x)| \leq |S_m(x) - f(x)| + |f(x) - S_N(x)| < 2\varepsilon.$$

This holds for **every** $x \in \mathbb{R}$, so the polynomial

$$P(x) := S_m(x) - S_N(x) = \sum_{k=N+1}^{m} a_k (x-c)^k$$

is bounded on $\mathbb{R}$.

**Key observation.** A polynomial that is bounded on all of $\mathbb{R}$ must be constant. But $P(x)$ has no constant term: every summand has $(x-c)^k$ with $k \geq N+1 \geq 1$, so $P(c) = 0$. A constant polynomial that vanishes at a point is identically zero. Therefore

$$P(x) \equiv 0, \quad \text{i.e.,} \quad a_{N+1} = a_{N+2} = \cdots = a_m = 0.$$

Since $m > N$ was arbitrary, we conclude

$$a_k = 0 \quad \text{for all } k > N.$$

Hence $f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{N} a_k(x-c)^k$ is a polynomial of degree at most $N$.

---

### Proof of Sufficiency

Conversely, suppose only finitely many $a_k$ are nonzero; say $a_k = 0$ for all $k > d$. Then $f(x) = S_d(x)$, and for every $n \geq d$,

$$\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |f(x) - S_n(x)| = 0.$$

The partial sums are eventually identical to $f$, so the series converges uniformly (in fact, trivially) on $\mathbb{R}$.

---

### Conclusion

The power series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k(x-c)^k$ converges uniformly on $(-\infty, \infty)$ **if and only if** it terminates, i.e., there exists $d \geq 0$ such that $a_k = 0$ for all $k > d$. In other words, the only power series converging uniformly on the entire real line are **polynomials**.

The essential reason is that any non-terminating power series with infinite radius of convergence defines a transcendental entire function, whose Taylor polynomials are unbounded on $\mathbb{R}$ (being non-constant polynomials), making uniform approximation on the unbounded domain $\mathbb{R}$ impossible.
